en: The regional (dēśī) language is generally difficult to compose, and even when composed, it is hard to understand;
therefore, Ācārya Hemacandra composes and analyzes it.

While the grammatical instruction of all words was intended to be undertaken, the grammatical instruction of the six languages, beginning with Sanskrit, has been completed in the work named *Siddhahemacandra*. Now, there remain regional (*deśya*) words that were not previously established by earlier authorities through the sequential processes of elision, augmentation, and modification of phonemes. This work is commenced for the purpose of collecting those. At the outset, the presiding deity is saluted according to the convention of the learned:
"Deep as the ocean of the *gamana*, *nayana*, and *pramāṇa* [the three types of inference], possessing the secret that enters the hearts of the wise..."
Victorious is the speech of the Lords of Jinas, which transforms into all possible languages. // DēNāMā.1 // 1 //

The *nayās* are specific perspectives that do not contradict the *syādvāda*, which possess similar readings yet differ in their underlying intent (*tātparya*), as they grasp only a single portion of the reality (*vastu*). They are designated as *naigama*, *saṅgraha*, *vyavahāra*, *ṛjusūtra*, *śabda*, *samabhirūḍha*, and *evambhūta*. The seven means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*)—perception and the rest—have the *syādvāda* as their domain; by these [means], the doctrine is profound and unfathomable to those of dull intellect. Nevertheless, it is "heart-captivating" (*hr̥dayaṅgama*), meaning its secret essence touches the hearts of those who possess a sensitive and conscious heart. For this very reason, it "triumphs," meaning it exists with superiority over the doctrines of all other sectarians (*tīrthikas*). Furthermore, the act of salutation is implied by the sense of "triumph. Another excellence is that it transforms itself into the form of every language. As it has been said: "The gods speak in divine speech, men in human, and even the Śabaras in the Śabara tongue."
For even the animals understood the speech of the Blessed One in their own animal tongue.
The connection is that such is the speech of the Lords of Jinas or the Arhats, and it is victorious.
To prompt the engagement of those desiring to understand, he states the subject matter and the purpose:
"Because of being agitated by curiosity, which has blossomed with the fragrance of the entire region... [1]
The *Deśīśabdasangraha*, arranged according to the order of the vowels, is now being composed. // 2 // DēNāMā.2

By the term *dēśī* (regional/local), the *dēśī* treatises are meant. Because of the "fragrance" (*parimala*)—that is, the thorough study—of all *dēśī* treatises, there arose a curiosity that was in some cases frustrated by the failure of words to convey their meanings, in some by the absence of certainty regarding the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*), in some by contradictions with earlier *dēśī* authorities, and in some by the adherence to words and meanings merely through blind imitation (*gatānugatikatā*). Driven by the agitation caused by that curiosity—the impetuous desire to benefit others, thinking, "How may this people, who are submerged in the mud of corrupt (*apabhraṣṭa*) words, be rescued?"—this compilation of *dēśī* forms of words is being composed. The phrase "by us" (*asmābhiḥ*) is to be supplied as the agent. Regarding the purpose for undertaking this work despite the existence of *dēśī* treatises composed by Pādaliptācārya and others, the author states it by way of a qualification: "of phonemes" (*vaṇṇa-*) and so forth. "Phonemes" (*varṇāḥ*) are those beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, suitable for usage in Prākṛt. Their "sequence" (*kramaḥ*) is the orderly arrangement for the sake of easy grasping and retention when they form the beginnings of words. It is "easy" or "auspicious" (*sukhadaḥ subhagaḥ*) by virtue of that sequence of phonemes and the sequence of words consisting of two, three, four, or more syllables. For words indicated according to the sequence of phonemes are easily remembered and determined when doubts arise regarding specific meanings; whereas words indicated by disregarding the sequence of phonemes cannot be easily determined. Thus, the indication according to the sequence of phonemes is meaningful. [2]
Furthermore, he states the distinction from those belonging to other regions:

"Those characteristics which are neither established nor well-known among the names in Sanskrit, and for which there is no possibility of being figurative characteristics or etymological derivations—those have been recorded here. (Dēvīnāmamālā 3)

In this work titled *Siddhahemacandra*, which is a treatise on grammar (*lakṣaṇa*), those words that were not established—that is, not derived—through the analysis of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) have been compiled here. However, those such as *bajjara*, *pajjara*, *upphāla*, *pisuṇa*, *saṅgha*, *bōlla*, *cava*, *jampa*, *sīsa*, *sāha*, and so forth—which were established in the *Siddhahemacandra* (4.2) as substitutes (*ādeśa*) for words like *kathya*—have not been included by us here, even though they are accepted by others among the regional (*deśī*) words. Furthermore, those words which, despite being established through the analysis of roots and suffixes, are not well-known in the Sanskrit lexicons (*abhidhānakōśa*) have also been included here. For example: *amr̥tanirgama*, *chinnōdbhavā*, *aprahānaṭā*, and so on, used in the senses of "moon," "dūrvā grass," "Śiva" (*hara*), and so forth. Also, those which, though not well-known in the Sanskrit lexicons, are possible through figurative (*gauṇī*) or indicative (*lakṣaṇā*) power as explained in the *Alaṅkāracūḍāmaṇi*—such as *baïllō* for a fool, or the word *gaṅgā* for the bank of the Ganges—these have not been included here in this collection of regional words. [3]
Now, for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) into the various languages well-known in different regions, the definition of regional (*dēśī*) [words] is provided.
